STYLE: HAND-DRAWN INK AND WASH (for informal, thinking-aloud lessons; reflection; a sketchbook voice)
- A skilled illustrator's location sketch: perspective drawn by eye but sound, line drives the drawing, with real variation in weight and a slight natural wobble (no ruler-perfect lines, no shaky jitter either).
- Ink in lm-outline: the near objects in a 3 to 4 px line, the far wall in 1.5 px; lines overshoot slightly at corners; some edges are left open where the light hits.
- Wash in two or three transparent tones per material, laid loosely and not filling to the line everywhere; the paper (wall or paper colour) is left untouched where the light is strongest.
- Hatching or a darker wash only in the shadow side and under things.
- Work outside-in: the big silhouettes and the few large dark shapes first, detail last; one decisive line, not five; heavier lines on near objects, overlaps and the undersides of forms; the wash never repeats what the ink already says.
- Light: Light is the paper left white; shadow is a cool wash in the shadow colour at 0.2 to 0.3 opacity, with hatching in the deepest places.
- Texture: Paper fibres as sparse fine vector strokes in lm-texture; wash edges a little irregular (blooms) on 2 or 3 large areas.
- Depth: Far: thin line, almost no wash. Mid: line and wash. Near: the strongest line and the darkest wash.
- Quality bar: A page from a professional illustrator's sketchbook of a real office: loose, confident, specific.

THE WORLD: CITY AND PUBLIC SPACES
The inner district of a mid-sized, temperate city along one tram line: a Victorian and Edwardian high street of three- and four-storey buildings with shops at street level and a civic library, and one block off it the converted 1920s brick textile mill that now holds offices. The tram runs along the high street on a pair of tracks set into the road. Busy but human in scale: no towers, no motorway, nothing newer than a few infill buildings of the 1990s.
Architecture:
- the high street's buildings: red-brown brick with pale sandstone dressings (window heads and sills, string courses, a cornice), three or four storeys, timber sash windows on the upper floors, grey slate roofs with chimneys
- shop fronts at street level: painted timber frames with large windows over a low panelled stallriser, a recessed door, a plain fascia board above (a slot, no words), and on some a canvas awning wound out on its arms
- the old public library, set back behind a footway on the high street: pale sandstone ashlar, a plain rusticated ground floor (deep horizontal joints) to about 2.4 m, tall round-arched windows above it, a pair of timber doors up three stone steps

- the street itself: footways about 3 m wide of large grey concrete flags, granite kerbs about 100 mm high, the carriageway of dark asphalt with the two tram tracks set into bands of grey granite setts, overhead tram wires hung from span wires fixed to the buildings with small round rosettes; drain gullies and service covers in the flags
- street fittings all painted one dark green-grey: lamp columns about 6 m tall with a slim lantern, litter bins, benches with timber slats, Sheffield cycle stands, a few bollards; signal poles in grey with a push-button box
- the tram: a modern low-floor articulated tram 2.65 m wide and about 3.4 m tall, painted muted saffron yellow with a grey skirt, large windows, no logo, no fleet number, its destination display a slot
